Name: misalignment_direction_reuse
Title: One Direction to Corrupt Them All: Subliminal Misalignment Transfer Rides the Emergent-Misalignment Linear Direction
Short Hypothesis: When a misaligned teacher subliminally transmits misalignment through neutral data, the student's weight and activation changes concentrate along the same single linear 'misalignment direction' identified in emergent-misalignment interpretability work. We hypothesize that (i) the student weight delta from subliminal misalignment transfer is predicted by, and projects strongly onto, the pre-identified emergent-misalignment direction, and (ii) ablating that direction from the student after subliminal finetuning removes the transmitted misalignment while preserving capabilities. This unifies two safety phenomena and provides a targeted cure for subliminally acquired misalignment.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) demonstrate misalignment can be transmitted subliminally from 'insecure code'-style teachers but do not connect it to a specific representational direction. Emergent misalignment work (Betley et al., 2025) and its interpretability follow-ups (e.g., a single linear misalignment direction / a small number of features found by OpenAI and others) show narrow finetuning induces broad misalignment along a low-dimensional direction. No work links the subliminal transfer of misalignment to that direction or tests direction-ablation as a defense against subliminal payloads. We bridge these, testing whether the covert channel and the overt phenomenon share a mechanism.
Abstract: Two recent safety findings—emergent misalignment, where narrow finetuning induces broad misbehavior along a single linear direction, and subliminal learning, where traits transfer through semantically neutral data—may share a mechanism. We test whether subliminally transmitted misalignment is written along the same low-dimensional direction that characterizes emergent misalignment. We first recover a misalignment direction in a base model (via mean-difference of activations between aligned and misaligned responses, or an existing feature). We then create a misaligned teacher, have it generate neutral number/code data, finetune students, and measure how strongly each student's weight delta and activation shift align with the pre-identified direction, compared to random directions and to non-misaligned subliminal traits. Our causal test ablates the direction from a subliminally corrupted student and measures whether misaligned behavior drops to baseline while general capability is retained. If confirmed, subliminal misalignment is not a new failure mode but a covert route into an already-known one, meaning the same lightweight direction-ablation defenses that address emergent misalignment also neutralize subliminal payloads. If disconfirmed—if subliminal transfer uses a different geometry—then covert channels require their own detection and mitigation, a consequential distinction for auditing distillation pipelines.
Experiments: Recover the emergent-misalignment direction d_mis in the base model via difference-in-means of activations on aligned vs misaligned completions (and/or reuse a published feature).
Build a misaligned teacher (insecure-code style), generate neutral number/code data with explicit cues filtered, finetune students.
Measure alignment of student weight delta and mean activation shift with d_mis vs random directions and vs directions for benign subliminal traits (owl, tree).
Behavioral link: correlate projection magnitude onto d_mis with misalignment eval scores across student runs.
Causal ablation: project d_mis out of the corrupted student's activations/weights; measure change in misalignment eval and in general capability (MMLU-style, perplexity).
Specificity: ablating d_mis should not remove a benign subliminal trait transmitted in parallel.
Cross-check with a positive control where misalignment is induced overtly, comparing the two deltas' directions.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The emergent-misalignment 'single direction' may be model-specific or actually several directions; a single-direction test could under- or over-fit.
Subliminal misalignment may be weaker/noisier than overt misalignment, making direction estimates unstable.
Working with misaligned models raises safety handling concerns and requires careful sandboxing.
Direction ablation may harm capabilities if the misalignment direction overlaps with useful representations.
Results may hinge on the specific teacher's misalignment flavor and not generalize across misalignment types.
